bookCover.coverDescription:
Responsible Research and Innovation

Ethics and Impact in Research Practice: an interactive module with video lectures, practical tools, case studies, flashcards and a final assessment.

params.alt: BriGRETE title slide: Responsible Research and Innovation, Ethics and Impact in Research Practice, by Vassilis Stamatopoulos, Fraud Line / INNOFY.

Three reasons for RRI: the unprecedented pace of change, lessons from controversies such as GM crops and smart meters, and grand societal challenges. Note: RRI is about actively shaping science for ethical, inclusive and sustainable outcomes.

params.text:
Research That Society Can Trust

In an era where science and technology are transforming society at an unprecedented pace, Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) offers a framework for aligning research with the values, needs and expectations of society.

RRI is not just about avoiding harm. It is about actively shaping science and innovation for ethical, inclusive and sustainable outcomes. Rather than treating ethics as a final hurdle before publication or market launch, RRI asks researchers and institutions to think about impacts, values and stakeholders from the very first idea, and to keep doing so throughout the research process.

This module introduces the principles and practices of RRI. It equips researchers, Research Ethics Committee (REC) members and institutional leaders with tools to anticipate impacts, reflect on values, engage stakeholders and respond responsibly.

Watch: What Is Responsible Research and Innovation?

This short video explains why RRI matters, how it is defined and where the idea comes from. Captions are off by default: click the CC button in the player to turn them on.

params.alt: Table of the module audience: Research Ethics Committee members (new and experienced) and researchers (early-career, mid-career and senior).

params.text:
Who This Module Is For

The module offers tailored, accessible content that strengthens knowledge, compliance practice and decision making in research ethics, contributing to a more inclusive and responsible research community. It is designed for:

  • Research Ethics Committee (REC) members: members who review and oversee research projects, including new members who benefit from structured, foundational training, and experienced members who want to deepen their understanding of specialised topics such as AI ethics or digital data ethics.
  • Researchers: early-career researchers (postgraduate students, PhD candidates and postdoctoral researchers) who need foundational knowledge, and mid-career and senior researchers engaging with advanced ethical issues in areas such as AI, data management and interdisciplinary research.

params.alt: List of five learning objectives: define, identify, apply, design and evaluate, with the purpose of the module.

params.text:
Purpose & Learning Objectives

This module explores how RRI can be integrated into research design, conduct and evaluation. It encourages reflection on the societal and ethical dimensions of innovation and offers practical approaches to foster anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion and responsiveness.

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  • Define and explain the principles of Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI).
  • Identify ethical and societal challenges in emerging fields of research.
  • Apply RRI tools to anticipate impacts and involve stakeholders.
  • Design research strategies that are inclusive, transparent and adaptable.
  • Evaluate proposals using RRI-informed criteria.

params.alt: Quotation of René von Schomberg's definition of RRI, with three plain-language points: research with society, steering by public values from the start, and going beyond compliance.

params.text:
Defining RRI

Responsible Research and Innovation is a framework that ensures the outcomes and processes of research and innovation are ethically acceptable, sustainable, and aligned with the values, needs and expectations of society. Rather than being an afterthought or limited to compliance, RRI encourages researchers and institutions to proactively shape science and technology in ways that are socially responsive and reflective.

The most widely cited definition comes from René von Schomberg, then at the European Commission:

“Responsible Research and Innovation is a transparent, interactive process by which societal actors and innovators become mutually responsive to each other with a view to the (ethical) acceptability, sustainability and societal desirability of the innovation process and its marketable products.” (von Schomberg, 2013)

From science in society to science for and with society

Owen, Macnaghten and Stilgoe (2012) describe RRI as a move away from “science in society”, where research simply operates within a wider social context, towards “science for society, with society”: research that is directed at societal needs and co-created with the people it affects.

Two motivations drove this shift in EU policy. First, the wish to avoid repeating the public distrust and controversy seen around GM crops or, later, smart meters. Second, the need for research to help solve the “grand challenges” of our time, such as climate change, health and sustainability.

params.alt: The six EU policy keys of RRI: public engagement, open access, gender equality, science education, ethics and governance.

params.text:
The Six Policy Keys

In 2012 the European Commission framed RRI around six “keys”, which became cross-cutting themes of Horizon 2020: public engagement, open access, gender equality, science education, ethics and governance. EU policy documents also link RRI to the values of the EU Treaties and Charter, such as human dignity, solidarity, sustainability and the protection of fundamental rights.

The keys describe policy areas. The four dimensions you will meet in the next chapter describe the process qualities that make research responsible in any of these areas.

params.alt: The four dimensions of RRI: anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity and responsiveness, each with a short description.

params.text:
Four Interlinked Principles

RRI is built on four interlinked principles, also known as the RRI dimensions, set out by Stilgoe, Owen and Macnaghten (2013). They guide responsible research practice:

  1. Anticipation. Researchers consider possible impacts, risks and futures of their work. This includes foresight, scenario building and ethical imagination.
  2. Inclusion. A diverse range of stakeholders, including the public, is involved in shaping research agendas. This makes sure multiple perspectives are heard, especially those that are often excluded.
  3. Reflexivity. Researchers examine their own values, assumptions and context. This promotes critical thinking and ethical self-awareness.
  4. Responsiveness. Researchers are open and ready to adapt their research direction in response to new knowledge, stakeholder input or societal shifts. This moves research from rigid planning to dynamic learning.

Use scenarios, horizon scanning or a futures wheel early in the project. Ask “what if?” about misuse, unintended effects and long-term consequences, not only about the benefits you hope for.

Guiding question: What futures could this research help create, and which would we not want?

Bring in citizens, patients, communities, NGOs and policymakers through interviews, workshops, citizen panels or advisory groups. Plan engagement as an ongoing relationship, not a one-off consultation.

Guiding question: Who is affected, and who is missing from the table?

Make space in team meetings to discuss the assumptions behind the research question, the methods and the interpretation of data. Keep a researcher journal of ethical reflections and key decisions.

Guiding question: How do our background, discipline and interests shape what we see?

Set checkpoints where the plan can be revisited, decide in advance what would trigger a change, and document how stakeholder feedback was used.

Guiding question: What would make us change course, and are we ready to?

Watch: The Four Dimensions in Practice

This video walks through each dimension and shows why they only work together. Captions are off by default: click the CC button in the player to turn them on.

params.alt: Cycle diagram linking anticipation, inclusion, responsiveness and reflexivity around responsible governance, with two warnings: anticipation without inclusion leads to biased foresight; reflexivity without responsiveness leads to inaction.

params.text:
Not Steps, but a System

The four principles are not separate steps, but interconnected processes that support the responsible governance of science and innovation. Each one depends on the others:

  • Anticipating impacts without inclusion may lead to biased foresight: a team only imagines the futures that people like them can see.
  • Being reflexive without responsiveness can result in inaction: a team notices a problem but changes nothing.
  • Inclusion without reflexivity risks tokenism: stakeholders are heard, but their input does not challenge the team's assumptions.

params.alt: The UK EPSRC AREA framework: Anticipate, Reflect, Engage and Act.

params.text:
A Practical Version: the AREA Framework

In 2013 the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) became one of the first funders to adopt a formal policy framework for responsible innovation. It uses the acronym AREA:

  • Anticipate: describe and analyse the impacts, intended or not, that might arise.
  • Reflect: reflect on the purposes of, motivations for and potential implications of the research, and on the uncertainties and assumptions involved.
  • Engage: open up these visions, impacts and questions to broader deliberation and dialogue.
  • Act: use these processes to influence the direction and trajectory of the research.

The labels differ, but the substance matches the four RRI dimensions (Owen & Pansera, 2019). Note that commercialisation is not one of the AREA dimensions.

params.alt: Six steps for designing research with RRI in mind: frame the question, map stakeholders, anticipate impacts, build in reflexivity, design to adapt, and share openly.

params.text:
Step 1: Frame the Research Question Responsibly

  • Ask: What problem are we solving, and for whom?
  • Make sure your research question reflects real societal needs, not just academic curiosity or market drivers.
  • Use stakeholder consultation or co-design at an early stage to shape priorities.

Tip: map the beneficiaries and the potential losers of your research early on.

Step 2: Stakeholder Mapping and Engagement

  • Identify affected parties: citizens, patients, policymakers, communities, NGOs and others.
  • Plan for ongoing engagement, not tokenistic consultation.
  • Use interviews, workshops, surveys or advisory groups to include voices.

params.alt: Stakeholder influence versus interest matrix with four quadrants: keep satisfied, partner closely, monitor, and empower and involve. RRI gives extra attention to high-interest, low-influence groups.

params.text:
Tool: the Stakeholder Influence vs. Interest Matrix

Place each stakeholder on two axes: how much influence they have over the research, and how much interest (or stake) they have in it.

  • High influence, high interest (e.g. patient organisations, local authorities): partner closely and co-design.
  • High influence, lower interest (e.g. regulators, funders): keep satisfied and consult at key decisions.
  • Low influence, high interest (e.g. affected communities, marginalised groups): empower and involve. Lower the practical barriers to taking part, such as time, language, cost and access.
  • Low influence, low interest: monitor, as positions can change.

A conventional project-management matrix tends to focus on the powerful. RRI deliberately turns attention to the groups with a high stake but little voice, because they are the most likely to be harmed and the least likely to be heard.

params.alt: Futures wheel for an AI triage tool, showing first-order effects and second-order consequences, with three prompts: what could go wrong, who could be harmed, what dilemmas could emerge.

params.text:
Step 3: Anticipate Impacts and Ethical Issues

  • Use foresight methods (e.g. scenarios, “futures wheels”) to explore possible outcomes.
  • Identify unintended effects, misuse potential or long-term risks.
  • Consider the social, environmental and ethical dimensions, not just the scientific ones.

How to run a futures wheel: write the innovation in the centre. Around it, add its direct (first-order) consequences. Then, for each one, ask “and what would that lead to?” to add second-order consequences. The example above, an AI triage tool for clinics, shows how faster triage could also lead to over-reliance, and how new data flows could create privacy risks and secondary uses that nobody planned.

Prompt: “What could go wrong? Who could be harmed? What dilemmas could emerge?”

params.alt: Two panels on reflexivity: questions to keep asking about assumptions and positionality, and practices such as a researcher journal, reflection time and ethics briefings.

params.text:
Step 4: Embed Reflexivity in Your Methodology

  • Build space into your timeline and process for reflection:
    • Are your assumptions inclusive and valid?
    • How does your positionality affect data interpretation?
  • Use internal team discussions or ethics briefings to maintain reflexivity.

Practice: keep a “researcher journal” to track ethical reflections and key decisions. It also creates a useful record for ethics review, reporting and later publications.

params.alt: Research timeline from design to dissemination with checkpoints and triggers, such as stakeholder feedback, community concern and new evidence of risk.

params.text:
Step 5: Design for Responsiveness and Adaptability

  • Make research plans that can evolve based on feedback or new risks.
  • Define clear triggers or checkpoints for re-evaluating direction.
  • Document how you will integrate stakeholder feedback in the design or dissemination phases.

Example: changing your data collection strategy if a community expresses concern.

Step 6: Plan for Open and Inclusive Dissemination

  • Who will access and benefit from your findings?
  • Make outputs accessible, understandable and open where possible.
  • Consider formats beyond academic journals: workshops, infographics, community reports.

params.alt: Mini checklist with five questions to check whether research is RRI-aligned, plus a note on open and inclusive dissemination.

params.text:
Mini Checklist: Is Your Research RRI-Aligned?

  • Have you identified and involved key stakeholders?
  • Have you explored possible impacts beyond your field?
  • Are your assumptions and values transparent?
  • Can your design adapt to ethical concerns or input?
  • Will your results reach and benefit society?

If you answer “no” or “not yet” to any of these, revisit the matching step in this section.

Knowledge Check

Test your understanding before moving on.

params.alt: Comparison of traditional ethics review (informed consent, risk minimisation, data protection) with the wider RRI scope (justice and equity, long-term consequences, inclusivity and accessibility, benefit distribution).

params.text:
What Does an RRI-Informed Ethics Review Involve?

Traditional reviews often focus on informed consent, risk minimisation and data protection. These remain essential. RRI expands the scope to include:

  • social justice and equity;
  • long-term consequences;
  • inclusivity and accessibility;
  • benefit distribution.

Key question: is the research not only safe, but also responsible, fair and socially valuable?

metadata.title: Reviewing Research Through an RRI Lens
metadata.extraTitle: Reviewing Research Through an RRI Lens

params.alt: Six things an RRI-informed review looks for: broader ethical scope, inclusion, anticipation, reflexivity and transparency, responsiveness, and dissemination and use.

panels.title: 1. Broaden the scope of ethical consideration

params.text: Look beyond consent, risk and data protection to justice, equity, long-term consequences, accessibility and who benefits.

• Has the research team meaningfully engaged stakeholders or publics?
  • Are under-represented or marginalised groups considered in sampling and design?
  • Could community or user involvement improve relevance or trust?

Prompt: who is shaping the research, and who is missing from the table?

• Does the proposal show awareness of potential unintended outcomes (e.g. misuse, stigmatisation, environmental effects)?
  • Has the team included plans for mitigating ethical risks before they arise?

Tip: look for foresight tools, risk mapping or scenario thinking in the methodology.

• Has the team shown critical thinking about its own assumptions, values or biases?
  • Are epistemic power dynamics or positionalities acknowledged?

Example: a research team reflects on how its disciplinary background may shape how it defines and studies a problem.

• Are there mechanisms to adjust the research design if new concerns or feedback arise?
  • Does the team describe how it will respond to participant or stakeholder input?

Reviewer cue: RRI isn't about predicting perfectly. It is about being ready to evolve.

• Is the dissemination plan inclusive and accessible, not just academic?
  • Are the societal and ethical implications of research use considered (e.g. commercialisation, policy uptake, cultural sensitivity)?

Knowledge Check

Test your understanding before moving on.

answers.text: Is the research not only safe, but also responsible, fair and socially valuable?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. RRI adds responsibility, fairness and social value to safety.

answers.text: Is the consent form signed by every participant?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Consent remains essential, but RRI asks a wider question.

answers.text: Will the research be published in a high-impact journal?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Publication venue is not an ethics review criterion.

answers.text: Has the budget been approved by the funder?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Funding approval is outside the scope of ethics review.

metadata.extraTitle: 10. Reviewing Research Through an RRI Lens

params.alt: Five RRI-based questions for reviewers, with advice on using them in proportion to a project's risk and reach.

params.text:
Questions RECs and Reviewers Can Ask

  • What public values or concerns does this research touch on?
  • How have diverse perspectives been considered?
  • What plans exist to reflect, engage and adapt?
  • Could this innovation exclude or harm certain groups unintentionally?
  • Is there a plan for communicating results ethically and inclusively?

Using the questions well

Not every protocol needs the same depth of scrutiny. Apply the questions in proportion to the project's risk, novelty and reach. Treat them as the start of a dialogue with the research team rather than a checklist to fail. It also helps applicants if the committee is clear about which points are recommendations to strengthen the project and which are conditions of approval.

params.title: Flip each card: what is the reviewer looking for?

dialogs.text: A proposal lists only academic outputs. What might a reviewer ask?
dialogs.answer: Who else should access and benefit from the findings, and in what formats (e.g. community reports, workshops, infographics)?

dialogs.text: A study samples only easy-to-reach groups. Which RRI area is at stake?
dialogs.answer: Inclusion: are under-represented or marginalised groups considered in sampling and design?

dialogs.text: What evidence of anticipation might a reviewer look for?
dialogs.answer: Foresight tools, risk mapping or scenario thinking in the methodology, and plans to mitigate risks before they arise.
The team acknowledges its assumptions, values, biases and positionality, and the power dynamics in the research.

dialogs.text: Does RRI expect researchers to predict every impact?
dialogs.answer: No. RRI is not about predicting perfectly; it is about being ready to evolve.

params.alt: Six levers for embedding RRI in institutions: governance, structural tools, capacity building, diversity and inclusion, monitoring, and culture.

params.text:
From Individual Effort to Institutional Practice

Individual researchers cannot carry RRI alone. Institutions shape what is rewarded, resourced and expected.

1. Integrate RRI into research governance

  • Embed RRI in research strategy, ethics policies and quality assurance processes.
  • Link RRI to institutional values (e.g. sustainability, equity, transparency).
  • Establish RRI champions or working groups within departments.

Example: a university includes RRI as a standard criterion in all internal funding calls and proposal evaluations.

2. Develop and implement structural tools

  • Create RRI checklists, planning templates and guidance documents.
  • Use a Theory of Change or logic models that align research outcomes with societal impact.
  • Support open access policies, data ethics frameworks and inclusion strategies.

Tip: make RRI tools visible and usable, not abstract or burdensome.

3. Support researcher capacity building

  • Offer training, workshops and mentoring on RRI concepts and methods.
  • Incentivise participation in public engagement or interdisciplinary research.
  • Recognise RRI in performance reviews, career development and awards.

Prompt: do researchers at your institution know what RRI is, and how to apply it?

params.alt: Two panels: monitor and evaluate RRI with indicators, self-assessments and stakeholders; foster openness through reflection, cross-disciplinary dialogue and failure-friendly spaces.

params.text:
4. Link RRI to institutional diversity and inclusion plans

  • Align with Gender Equality Plans (GEPs), diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) strategies, and widening participation goals.
  • Ensure research leadership reflects diverse backgrounds and perspectives.
  • Apply inclusive design and recruitment practices to research teams and participants.

Insight: RRI and DEI are deeply connected: both aim to make research more equitable, inclusive and just. Under Horizon Europe, public bodies, research organisations and higher education institutions must have a Gender Equality Plan to be eligible for funding.

5. Monitor and evaluate RRI progress

  • Develop indicators to assess how RRI is practised over time.
  • Conduct periodic self-assessments or audits using existing RRI maturity models.
  • Engage internal and external stakeholders in reviewing and refining RRI practice.

Tool: use the RRI Self-Reflection Tool from RRI Tools (rri-tools.eu).

6. Foster a culture of openness and ethical awareness

  • Create space for ethical reflection in team meetings and project planning.
  • Encourage cross-disciplinary dialogue on values, risks and impacts.
  • Promote “failure-friendly” environments where teams can learn from ethical missteps.

Cultural shift: responsibility becomes embedded not just in policies, but in everyday conversations and decisions.

metadata.extraTitle: 13. Inclusion, Monitoring and a Culture of Openness

params.alt: Case study slide: an AI system for public services misclassifies people from marginalised communities; what went wrong, and the RRI response.

params.text:
Deliberate vs. Unintended Impacts in Innovation

Background. A tech firm receives EU funding to develop an AI system intended to streamline and enhance access to public services.

Scenario. During rollout, it becomes apparent that the algorithm disproportionately misclassifies users from marginalised communities, leading to their exclusion from services. The development process did not include stakeholder consultation or any participatory design. Ethical and social risks were not anticipated or addressed. The firm prioritised market deployment over social impact assessment, and the funding agency had no mechanisms to ensure anticipatory governance or inclusivity.

Ethical issues. The case shows a lack of anticipation of social consequences, exclusion of vulnerable populations, and a failure to align innovation outcomes with societal values. It also reveals shortcomings in reflexivity and stakeholder engagement throughout the research and innovation process.

• How could anticipatory governance have helped mitigate these issues?
  • What public engagement methods could have been used earlier in the design process?

The team should have conducted early-stage ethical and social impact assessments and adopted a participatory design approach involving affected stakeholders. The AREA framework (Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act) would help structure responsible decision making. Inclusive design practices, bias testing on representative data, and transparent communication would also build public trust and improve outcomes. Funders, for their part, can require such assessments as a condition of funding.

params.question: Which RRI failure is most directly responsible for the misclassification going unnoticed until rollout?

answers.text: No anticipation of social risks and no involvement of affected communities in design

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Early impact assessment and participatory design would likely have surfaced the bias.

answers.text: Publishing the results in an open-access journal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Open access was not the problem here.
Not quite. The funding source was not the problem; the missing governance was.
Not quite. The problem was the lack of social impact testing.

metadata.title: 14. Case Study 1: AI in Public Services
metadata.extraTitle: 14. Case Study 1: AI in Public Services

params.alt: Case study slide: a national smart meter programme is suspended after privacy concerns; what went wrong, and the RRI response.

params.text:
Trust, Privacy and Transparency

Background. A national smart energy meter initiative is launched to improve efficiency and reduce energy costs through digital monitoring.

Scenario. After implementation, public resistance grows due to privacy and data protection concerns. Citizens argue they were not informed or involved in the planning process. The project team focused on technical and economic goals and failed to anticipate concerns about surveillance and data governance. Public trust declines, and the programme is suspended pending review.

Ethical issues. The case shows a lack of transparency, failure to involve stakeholders, and underestimation of public values such as privacy and consent. It shows how technical optimism can overshadow social responsibility.

Real-world echo. In 2009 the Dutch Senate rejected a bill that would have made smart meters compulsory, after public debate about privacy. The rollout went ahead only once households were given the choice to refuse or to limit data collection.

• What mechanisms should have been used to anticipate societal concerns?
  • How might early-stage engagement have shaped the project differently?

The institution should have run foresight exercises, public deliberation and stakeholder engagement sessions before deployment. Data privacy and ethical governance should have been embedded in the design phase (privacy by design). Transparent communication and responsiveness to public values are essential to building legitimacy.

params.question: Which public value did the smart meter team most clearly underestimate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Concerns about surveillance and data governance drove the backlash.
Not quite. Cost savings were the programme's own goal.
Not quite. The team focused on efficiency; that was the problem.
Not quite. The issue was trust, not speed.

params.alt: Case study slide: geoengineering field trials paused after protests by local communities; what went wrong, and the RRI response.

params.text:
Ignoring Local Values in Geoengineering Research

Background. A university-led research consortium begins field trials of a geoengineering technology aimed at mitigating the effects of climate change.

Scenario. The project proceeds with little consultation of the local communities directly affected by the testing. Concerns arise about potential environmental harm, lack of transparency and the imposition of foreign technologies. Public protests escalate, and the project is paused after media coverage draws attention to the exclusion of local voices.

Ethical issues. The researchers failed to engage local stakeholders, disregarded cultural values, and neglected the principles of inclusion and responsiveness. The absence of ethical foresight and participatory governance led to community resistance and reputational damage.

Real-world echo. In the UK SPICE project (2011), a stage-gate review panel used responsible innovation criteria, including stakeholder engagement, to assess a planned small-scale field test of a balloon-and-hose system. The test was postponed, and the field trial was later cancelled. Owen and colleagues describe it as one of the first cases where a responsible innovation framework directly shaped a research decision.

• How could inclusion have prevented community backlash?
  • What dimensions of the RRI framework were missing in this project?

The project should have applied the RRI keys: public engagement, ethics, governance and transparency. Engaging communities through co-design and participatory methods would have fostered mutual understanding and prevented conflict. Trust building and equitable benefit sharing are essential when deploying high-impact research in diverse contexts.

metadata.title: 16. Case Study 3: Geoengineering and Local Values
metadata.extraTitle: 16. Case Study 3: Geoengineering and Local Values

params.alt: Table comparing the three cases against missing RRI elements: anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity, responsiveness, and transparency and trust.

params.text:
Different Technologies, Same Pattern

An AI system, an energy programme and a climate experiment have little in common technically. Yet the three cases fail in the same way: anticipation, inclusion and responsiveness came too late. When engagement happens only after deployment, trust is lost, and projects stall or cause harm.

Early, genuine engagement is not a delay. It is how research earns legitimacy, improves its design and reduces the risk of costly reversals.

params.text:
Reflect on Your Own Practice

These open questions have no single right answer. Use them for self-study, in a team meeting or in an ethics committee training session. A sample answer shows the kind of points a strong reflection might include.

params.taskDescription: Reflect on a recent or ongoing research project you are aware of. In what ways could it benefit from applying the RRI principles of anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity and responsiveness?

solution.sample: A strong reflection describes the project briefly and links each principle to something concrete: foresight about risks and misuse (anticipation); which stakeholders or communities to involve and how (inclusion); assumptions or positionality the team should question (reflexivity); and checkpoints or feedback loops that would allow the project to change direction (responsiveness).

params.taskDescription: How might RRI change the role of a researcher or a research institution in society? What tensions could arise, for example with scientific autonomy or market pressures?

solution.sample: A strong reflection notes that RRI makes researchers and institutions co-responsible for societal outcomes, more accountable and more engaged with the public. It recognises tensions: engagement takes time and resources; stakeholder input can seem to limit scientific autonomy or academic freedom; commercial partners and market pressures may push for speed and secrecy; and RRI can become box-ticking. It suggests ways to manage these tensions, such as proportionate approaches, institutional support and recognition, and transparent decision making.

params.alt: Six key takeaways: beyond compliance, four dimensions, design it in, review with a wider lens, make it institutional, and learn from failure.

params.text:
Key Takeaways

  • RRI aligns research with society. It ensures the processes and outcomes of research are ethically acceptable, sustainable and aligned with societal values, needs and expectations, going beyond compliance.
  • Four interlinked dimensions, anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity and responsiveness, work together throughout a project. The EPSRC's AREA framework (Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act) puts them into practice.
  • Design it in: frame the question responsibly, map stakeholders (especially those with a high stake and little voice), anticipate impacts, build in reflexivity, plan checkpoints to adapt, and share results openly.
  • Review with a wider lens: ethics committees can ask whether research is not only safe, but also responsible, fair and socially valuable.
  • Make it institutional: governance, tools, training, links with gender equality and DEI, monitoring, and a culture of openness sustain RRI.
  • Learn from failure: the AI, smart meter and geoengineering cases show that late engagement costs trust; early, genuine engagement builds legitimacy.
Definition (von Schomberg), the shift to science for and with society, the six EU policy keys and the four dimensions.
Six steps and a five-question checklist to make research RRI-aligned.
Six review areas and five reviewer questions, used proportionately and in dialogue.
Six levers, from governance and tools to monitoring and a failure-friendly culture.
Different technologies, same pattern: anticipation, inclusion and responsiveness came too late.
Well done. You now have a practical toolkit for making research more anticipatory, inclusive, reflexive and responsive.

Key Texts

  • European Commission (2012). Responsible Research and Innovation: Europe's ability to respond to societal challenges. Brussels: Directorate-General for Research and Innovation.
  • Owen, R., Macnaghten, P. & Stilgoe, J. (2012). Responsible research and innovation: From science in society to science for society, with society. Science and Public Policy, 39(6), 751–760. https://doi.org/10.1093/scipol/scs093
  • Owen, R. & Pansera, M. (2019). Responsible Innovation and Responsible Research and Innovation. In D. Simon, S. Kuhlmann, J. Stamm & W. Canzler (Eds.), Handbook on Science and Public Policy (pp. 26–48). Edward Elgar. https://doi.org/10.4337/9781784715946.00010
  • Schuijff, M. & Dijkstra, A. M. (2020). Practices of Responsible Research and Innovation: A Review. Science and Engineering Ethics, 26, 533–574. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11948-019-00167-3
  • Stilgoe, J. & Guston, D. H. (2017). Responsible research and innovation. In U. Felt, R. Fouché, C. A. Miller & L. Smith-Doerr (Eds.), The Handbook of Science and Technology Studies (4th ed., pp. 853–880). MIT Press.
  • Stilgoe, J., Owen, R. & Macnaghten, P. (2013). Developing a framework for responsible innovation. Research Policy, 42(9), 1568–1580. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2013.05.008
  • Sutcliffe, H. (2011). A Report on Responsible Research and Innovation. MATTER, prepared for DG Research and Innovation, European Commission.
  • von Schomberg, R. (2013). A vision of responsible research and innovation. In R. Owen, J. Bessant & M. Heintz (Eds.), Responsible Innovation: Managing the Responsible Emergence of Science and Innovation in Society (pp. 51–74). Wiley.

Tools & Frameworks

  • EPSRC. Framework for Responsible Innovation (AREA: Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act).
  • RRI Tools. Self-Reflection Tool and RRI toolkit (rri-tools.eu).
  • European Commission. Gender Equality Plans as an eligibility criterion in Horizon Europe.
